claim: Stanford's contribution essay (2025-26, 100-250 words) is: 'Please describe what aspects of your life experiences, interests and character would help you make a distinctive contribution as an undergraduate to Stanford University.' This is a contribution/community-fit prompt that is open enough to carry post-SFFA identity material, and it asks what the student will GIVE, not what Stanford will give them.

application.content: Answer this as a contribution essay, not a 'why Stanford' essay: lead with a specific aspect of the writer's life experience / interest / character and the DISTINCTIVE thing it lets them bring to a dorm, lab, class, or club. Per the SFFA carve-out, identity or lived experience (including race, where it shaped the student) is fair game here ONLY when tied to how it shaped the person and what they'd contribute - not as a demographic label.

Strong signal: a reader can name one concrete thing the campus gains by admitting this student. Weak signal: the essay describes the student's qualities in the abstract ('I am hardworking and open-minded') without connecting them to a distinctive contribution - the prompt's operative word is 'distinctive,' so generic virtues fail it.

sources.citation: Application and Essays - Stanford Undergraduate Admission (contribution essay, 100-250 words)

connections.note: Stanford's contribution prompt is one instance of the post-SFFA community/contribution-prompt surge documented across the top 65 schools.
This prompt is a primary vehicle for the SFFA 'how race affected your life' carve-out; see the post-SFFA-identity subtopic for the legal frame and how-to. (Link target may not exist yet.)
